note: Leaves the left ventricle. The ascending aorta gives the coronary arteries; the arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian; it then descends through the thorax and abdomen and bifurcates at L4.
cl: the largest artery, leaving the left ventricle and bifurcating at L4

note: The first branch of the aortic arch, on the right only. It divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
cl: the first branch of the aortic arch, which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian

note: The left arises from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk. Each divides at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into the internal and external carotid arteries.
cl: it divides at about C4 into the internal and external carotid arteries

note: Ascends in the neck without branching, enters the skull through the carotid canal and supplies the brain and the orbit.
cl: it has no branches in the neck and enters the skull through the carotid canal

note: Supplies the face, scalp, neck and jaw. Its terminal branches are the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
cl: its terminal branches are the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries

note: A branch of the subclavian artery. It ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and enters the skull through the foramen magnum; the two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery.
cl: it runs through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and joins its partner to form the basilar artery

n: Circle of Willis and cerebral arteries
note: An anastomosis at the base of the brain that links the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. Drawn schematically here.
cl: an anastomotic ring at the base of the brain joining the carotid and vertebrobasilar supply

note: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and the aortic arch on the left. It becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.
cl: it becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib

note: Runs from the lateral border of the first rib to the inferior border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery.
cl: it runs from the first rib to the inferior border of teres major

note: Runs down the medial side of the arm and divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa. It is the usual artery for blood pressure measurement.
cl: it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa

note: Runs down the lateral forearm. Its pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis. It forms the deep palmar arch.
cl: its pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis

note: Runs down the medial forearm, gives off the common interosseous artery, and mainly forms the superficial palmar arch.
cl: it mainly forms the superficial palmar arch

note: The aorta bifurcates at L4 into the two common iliac arteries. Each divides at the pelvic brim, in front of the sacroiliac joint, into the internal and external iliac arteries.
cl: it divides at the pelvic brim into the internal and external iliac arteries

note: Supplies the pelvic organs, the gluteal region and the perineum.
cl: it supplies the pelvic organs, the buttock and the perineum

note: Runs along the pelvic brim and becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament.
cl: it becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament

note: Enters the thigh at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the popliteal artery. The profunda femoris is its main branch.
cl: it enters the thigh at the mid-inguinal point and passes through the adductor hiatus

note: The main supply to the thigh muscles. It arises laterally from the femoral artery just below the inguinal ligament.
cl: it is the main supply to the thigh muscles and arises just below the inguinal ligament

note: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee. It divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries at the lower border of popliteus.
cl: it runs behind the knee and divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries

note: Passes through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment and continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery.
cl: it continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery

note: Runs in the posterior compartment and passes behind the medial malleolus, where its pulse can be felt, before dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
cl: its pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus

note: Arises from the aorta at T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. It supplies the foregut.
cl: it arises at T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries

note: Arises from the aorta at L1 and supplies the midgut: from the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
cl: it arises at L1 and supplies the midgut

note: Arises from the aorta at L3 and supplies the hindgut: the distal third of the transverse colon down to the upper rectum.
cl: it arises at L3 and supplies the hindgut

note: Arises from the aorta at about L1 to L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery. The right is longer because the aorta lies to the left of the midline.
cl: it arises just below the superior mesenteric artery and the right is the longer one

note: A branch of the left coronary artery running in the anterior interventricular groove. It supplies the anterior left ventricle and most of the interventricular septum.
cl: it runs in the anterior interventricular groove

note: Arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove. It usually supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, and the SA and AV nodes.
cl: it arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove

note: A branch of the left coronary artery running in the left atrioventricular groove. It supplies the left atrium and the lateral and posterior left ventricle.
cl: it runs in the left atrioventricular groove

note: Formed behind the first right costal cartilage by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins. It drains the head, neck, upper limbs and thoracic wall into the right atrium.
cl: it is formed by the two brachiocephalic veins and drains into the right atrium

note: Formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The left is longer and crosses in front of the branches of the aortic arch to join the right and form the superior vena cava.
cl: it is formed by the internal jugular and subclavian veins and the left one is longer

note: Drains the brain and neck. It runs in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries and joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
cl: it runs in the carotid sheath and drains the brain and neck

note: The brachial veins (usually paired) accompany the brachial artery and unite to form the axillary vein, which becomes the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.
cl: the paired vessels that accompany the brachial artery

note: Formed by the union of the common iliac veins at L5. It ascends on the right of the aorta, passes through the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium.
cl: it is formed at L5 and passes through the diaphragm at T8

note: The external and internal iliac veins unite to form the common iliac vein. The two common iliac veins join at L5 to form the inferior vena cava.
cl: two of these join at L5 to form the inferior vena cava

note: Lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle (from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein). It is the continuation of the popliteal vein.
cl: it lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle

note: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It carries blood from the gut to the liver.
cl: it carries blood from the gut to the liver

note: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle. It divides under the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
cl: it carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle and divides into two

note: The right and left pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the lungs.
cl: it carries deoxygenated blood to a lung

note: Four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium. They are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood.
cl: it carries oxygenated blood from a lung to the left atrium

note: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6) and ends at the carina, at about the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5), where it divides into the right and left main bronchi. It is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage.
cl: a tube held open by C-shaped cartilage rings that divides at the carina

note: The trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi, which divide into lobar (secondary) bronchi (three on the right, two on the left) and then segmental bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies lodge there more often. Branching pattern drawn schematically.
cl: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left

note: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that runs from the pharynx (C6) behind the trachea and heart, passes through the diaphragm at T10 and joins the stomach at the cardia. The upper third is skeletal muscle, the lower third smooth muscle.
cl: a muscular tube that passes through the diaphragm at T10

note: Lies in the left upper quadrant. Its parts are the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus, with the lesser and greater curvatures. Rugae line the mucosa. The pylorus lies near the transpyloric plane (L1).
cl: a J-shaped organ with a fundus, body and pylorus, and greater and lesser curvatures

note: The first and shortest part of the small intestine (about 25 cm). It forms a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas and receives bile and pancreatic juice at the major duodenal papilla.
cl: a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas

note: Together about 3 to 5 m long in life. The jejunum (upper left) has prominent circular folds and the ileum (lower right) has Peyer patches; both are suspended on the mesentery and absorb most nutrients. Coiling is schematic.
cl: the coiled part of the small intestine suspended on the mesentery

note: Caecum, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, then rectum and anal canal. The colon has taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae; the ascending and descending parts are retroperitoneal.
cl: it has taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae

note: The largest solid organ, in the right hypochondrium under the diaphragm. It has right and left lobes, with the caudate and quadrate lobes on its visceral surface. It receives blood from the hepatic artery and portal vein.
cl: the largest solid organ, in the right hypochondrium

note: Stores and concentrates bile on the underside of the liver. Its fundus projects at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct.
cl: it stores bile and its fundus lies at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage

note: Lies retroperitoneally across L1 to L2 behind the stomach. It has a head (in the duodenal C-loop), neck, body and tail that reaches the splenic hilum. It has exocrine (digestive enzyme) and endocrine (islets of Langerhans) functions.
cl: a retroperitoneal gland with head, neck, body and tail, with exocrine and endocrine parts

note: Lies in the left upper quadrant behind the stomach, under ribs 9 to 11. It is the largest lymphoid organ and filters blood. A palpable spleen is enlarged.
cl: it lies under ribs 9 to 11 and filters blood

note: Retroperitoneal, either side of the vertebral column from about T12 to L3, with the right usually slightly lower because of the liver. Each has a cortex, medulla and renal pelvis, and the hilum transmits the renal vessels and ureter.
cl: a retroperitoneal organ with a cortex, medulla and renal pelvis

note: About 25 cm long. It runs down on psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder. Three constrictions: pelvicureteric junction, pelvic brim, and vesicoureteric junction.
cl: it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery

note: Lies behind the pubic symphysis when empty and rises into the abdomen as it fills. The trigone, a smooth triangle on the posterior wall, is bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
cl: it lies behind the pubic symphysis and has a smooth triangular trigone

note: Two lobes joined by an isthmus lying over the upper tracheal rings, at about C5 to T1. It makes thyroxine (T4), tri-iodothyronine (T3) and calcitonin.
cl: a gland of two lobes and an isthmus in front of the trachea

note: Sits on the upper pole of each kidney. The cortex makes corticosteroids (aldosterone, cortisol) and androgens; the medulla makes adrenaline and noradrenaline.
cl: it sits on the upper pole of the kidney, with a cortex and a medulla

n: Long thoracic, thoracodorsal and scapular nerves

note: Runs down the vertebral canal from the foramen magnum and ends at the conus medullaris at about L1 to L2 in adults; below that the lumbar and sacral nerve roots form the cauda equina.
cl: it ends at the conus medullaris at L1 to L2, below which is the cauda equina

note: Cerebrum (two hemispheres divided by the longitudinal fissure, with frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes), cerebellum and brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla). Surface folding is schematic.
cl: it has a cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem
